messages.subject: tracking progress of bears_optim_run
parts:
Hi Nick,

I'm trying to track the progress of a long BioGeoBEARS run.

I noticed that the output of calc_loglike_for_optim() gets printed many times as the run progresses, for example like this:

     d    e a b x n w u j ysv ys y s v mx01 mx01j mx01y mx01s mx01v mx01r  mf
1 0.01 0.01 0 1 0 0 1 0 0   3  2 1 1 1    0     0     0     0     0   0.5 0.1
  dp fdp      LnL
1  1   0 -379.485

It occurs to me that maybe one could count the number of times this has been printed (using grep), as use that to judge how far the function has progressed.

Is there any simple relationship between the number of times calc_loglike_for_optim() runs and the size of the input data (number of tips / ranges)?

Thanks!

Best,

Joel

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] tracking progress of bears_optim_run
parts:
Hi Joel,

My gut instinct is:

* If anything, more data (more species) should reduce the number of required optimization steps, because more data = a more peaked likelihood surface = easier optimization

* However, more species will slow down each individual likelihood calculation, although this is only a linear problem (double the species, double the time)

* Adding areas of course dramatically increases the calculation time (worse than quadratic)

* The different optimizers in R have different typical behaviors. For a 2-parameter problem (e.g. classic DEC), typically I recall seeing:

optim: 50-100 steps for optimization
optimx: 50-100 steps (but maybe a bit more than optim)
GenSA: perhaps 2x to 5x more steps

For all of these, each additional free parameter will likely ~double the number of steps required. But GenSA may have some minimum number of steps, it is Generalized Simulated Annealing, basically this is repeating the search again and again at different "temperatures", allowing bigger or smaller jumps between parameter guesses.  For large parameter spaces, GenSA is supposed to be better, and I think this seems to be typically true at even ~5-7 parameters, however someone did once post a case where GenSA in a 2-parameter problem never found an improvement beyond the starting d=0.01, e=0.01, whereas optimx rapidly found a better solution.

Beyond that, I don't know too much about how these work, these are all "off the shelf" optimizers available in base R (optim) or R packages (optimx, GenSA).

Cheers,
Nick
